newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: U.N. sees landmines on Geneva body agenda soon.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sees landmines on Geneva body agenda soon.

text.p: Momentum to ban land mines world-wide gathered on Thursday as a top U.N. official said the issue will almost certainly be on the agenda of a U.N. Conference on Disarmament in Geneva within two months.

"My expectation is that within a month or two we should find an agreement (to discuss landmines) on the agenda," U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Vladimir Petrovsky, who is also head of the Conference on Disarmament, told Reuters in an interview.
The Geneva body has 61 members including China and Russia -- two top mine producers and exporters.
As yet the only initiative underway is a Canadian effort, aiming for a legally binding agreement in December 1997 to ban the production, stockpiling, export, and use of land mines.
Petrovsky was in Vienna for a three-day conference on banning landmines, as part of the so-called "Ottawa process" begun last October at a 50-nation forum hosted by Canada.
Over 100 million land mines lie buried in 64 countries around the world. According to U.N. statistics land mines kill or maim a person every 20 minutes, or 25,000 people a year.
Anti-mine campaigners gained valuable publicity this year when Britain's Princess Diana took up the cause on a trip to war-ravaged Angola last month.

Many governments prefer the issue to be negotiated by the Geneva body, which will meet three times this year, as they regard Canada's deadline as unrealistic. Moreover China and Russia have not participated in the "Ottawa talks".

"I have a feeling there is growing support for the Conference on Disarmament, from what a number of delegations have said," Petrovsky noted. "The advantage is that all the 55 countries involved in the production of mines will be present."
But he said the two tracks -- Ottawa and the Conference on Disarmament -- should complement each other.
"It would be logical for the two processes to work hand in hand. It is necessary to use all routes leading to the prohibition of landmines," he said.

Petrovksy said the talks in Vienna were businesslike and specific, debating the scope of prohibition and the definition of anti-personnel mines. The issue of how to make countries comply with a ban will be discussed on Friday.
"The mood is generally optimistic, while some reservations were voiced," Petrovsky said. "There is an understanding that the conclusion of a treaty is a matter of urgency," he added.
Major mine producers such as the United States, Britain and France are among the delegates and India, Pakistan, Russia and Ukraine are present as observers. China declined to attend.
There are over 360 different types of anti-personnel mines, which explode underfoot, as opposed to anti-armour mines, designed to go off under the weight of heavy vehicles.
Petrovsky said the revised draft resulting from the forum could be expected to serve as a basis for future negotiations.
"We have a tremendous head start with a tentative treaty already worked out and that will speed up the whole process," he said.
Petrovsky was involved in the long wrangles over a nuclear test ban treaty, which took four years to complete and was finally signed last year.
A follow-up conference to the Vienna forum is planned in Brussels in June before a December meeting in Ottawa.
